followUps:
They talk through small, versioned messages instead of importing each other. The usual tools are browser CustomEvents on window, URL and route parameters, props handed down by the shell, or a tiny shared event bus.

Example: the catalog fires cart:add with {sku:"A1", qty:2}; the cart remote listens. Catalog never imports cart code, so either can deploy alone. Treat the payload like an API: version it, validate it, ignore unknown fields. Avoid one big shared global store, which becomes hidden coupling.

window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("cart:add",
  { detail: { sku: "A1", qty: 2 } }));

Use the strangler pattern: put a thin shell or edge router in front and move one route at a time from the old app to the new one.

  1. Add the shell; at first every path (for example /orders, /account) still goes to the Angular app.
  2. Pick a low-risk, high-value route, build it as a new remote, and switch only that path.
  3. Share login through a cookie so users do not sign in twice.
  4. Watch errors and speed, keep a flag to route back, then repeat.

When legacy traffic reaches 0%, delete the old app. Each route is a small, reversible step.

code.title: Module Federation share scope: pick the highest singleton version

followUps:
It happens when your entry file imports a shared library (such as React) directly, so the code runs before Module Federation has set up the share scope. The library is shared, but not yet available.

Fix: make the real entry file tiny and load everything through a dynamic import, which gives the runtime one async tick to negotiate versions. Setting eager: true also silences it, but then that library is bundled into the entry chunk and no longer shared properly.

// index.js
import("./bootstrap");
// bootstrap.js has the real imports (react, react-dom)

Keep every remote build immutable and versioned, and let the host find the current one through a small manifest read at run time. Rolling back then means editing the manifest, not rebuilding the host.

Example: the manifest says {"cart": "https://cdn.example.test/cart/1.8.2/remoteEntry.js"}. A bad release 1.8.3 is undone by pointing it back to 1.8.2. Serve the manifest with Cache-Control: no-cache so the change shows up within seconds. Also wrap each remote in an error boundary with a fallback UI, and use a feature flag so a broken remote can be switched off instantly.

code.title: Two React copies: hooks fail across instances, shared singleton works

followUps:
Any library that keeps identity-based state: react-dom, the router, state libraries, CSS-in-JS, i18n and data-fetching clients.

The rule: if a library uses React context, a global registry or a single store, two copies will not see each other. So share react, react-dom, react-router, react-redux or your store, @tanstack/react-query (its client lives in context), styled-components or emotion (theme and style injection), the i18n instance and your design-system package if it provides context. Pure helpers such as lodash or date-fns need not be singletons; sharing them only saves bytes.

If the host runs React 19 and a remote was built for 18, a singleton share gives a version warning (or an error with strictVersion), and if the remote falls back to its own React 18 you get the two-copy bug again.

React 19 removed old APIs such as ReactDOM.render, findDOMNode, propTypes checks and defaultProps on function components, so older remotes or libraries can break. Plan: first make remotes work on ^18 || ^19, test each remote against both in CI, upgrade remotes, then the shell, with a canary rollout.

code.title: Design tokens: three layers, theme mapping and contrast gate

followUps:
Set the theme before the browser paints, not in a React effect (effects run after the first paint, which causes the flash).

Put a tiny blocking script in <head> that reads the saved choice (cookie or localStorage) or prefers-color-scheme, and sets data-theme on <html>. Better, store the choice in a cookie so the server can render the attribute directly. Add <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> so the page background is right too. The CSS variables then match from the very first frame.

var t = localStorage.getItem("theme") ||
  (matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light");
document.documentElement.dataset.theme = t;

Add a brand layer on top of the semantic tokens, so each customer swaps values without touching components.

Store each tenant's choices as data (primary colour, radius, font), compile them to CSS variables scoped by attribute, for example [data-tenant="acme"] { --color-action: #0a7d4f; }, and load them at run time. Derive hover and active shades by code, and validate on upload: reject any colour pair under 4.5:1 contrast. Limit what can be overridden (colour, radius, font) and not layout. Cache the generated CSS per tenant.

First ask whether the need is real; then offer a supported way before anyone forks the component.

  • Slots or composition (pass children, an icon, a render prop).
  • Component-level tokens, such as overriding --button-radius.
  • A documented escape hatch like a className, which the library tracks.

If two or more teams ask for the same variant, promote it into the library through the intake process. If only one team needs it, they keep a small wrapper in their own repo and own it. Measure escape-hatch usage so you can see where the system is missing something.

It depends on where the 30 teams live. If they share one monorepo, consume the library as a workspace package; if they live in separate repos, publish it to a private npm registry.

Workspace: changes are instant, one pull request can change the library and fix every caller with a codemod, but everyone moves to the latest at the same time. Published: each team upgrades when ready and old versions keep working, but you now support several versions, and fixes take longer to reach everybody. Many companies do both: develop in the monorepo and publish to npm for outside consumers.

code.title: Affected detection and content-hash task cache

followUps:
The main risk is that the tool misses a dependency, so a broken package is never tested on the pull request and the failure shows up on main.

Typical causes: implicit links the graph cannot see (a shared config file, an environment variable, generated code, a dynamic import, runtime contracts between services), a wrong merge base, or a shallow git clone. Reduce it by treating root config changes as "affects everything", keeping the dependency graph checked by lint rules, running the full suite nightly and on main, and running a few end-to-end tests on every pull request regardless of what changed.

A cache key is a hash of everything that can change a task's output. If an input is missing from the key, the cache replays an old result that is wrong.

Inputs normally hashed: the package's source files, the hashes of the packages it depends on, config files (tsconfig.json), tool versions, chosen environment variables, and the command itself. Example: a build reads API_URL but it is not in the key, so a staging build is replayed for production (see the program). Fix by declaring inputs explicitly, keeping env names in the config, and spot-checking cached output against a fresh build.

"build": { "inputs": ["src/**", "tsconfig.json"], "env": ["API_URL"] }

Because skipWaiting() makes the new worker take over immediately, while open tabs still run old HTML and JavaScript that expect the old caches.

Example: a tab loaded with app.v1.js. The new worker activates and deletes the v1 cache. The user then clicks a route that lazy-loads chunk.v1.js; the file is gone from both cache and server, and the page breaks with a load error. Mixed versions (page v1, worker v2) cause subtle bugs too. Safer: let the new worker wait, show an "Update available" prompt, and call skipWaiting only when the user agrees, then reload on controllerchange.

Test them in a real browser, because service workers need a real browser engine (HTTPS or localhost). A Playwright or Puppeteer end-to-end test works well.

  1. Serve build v1, open the page, wait until the worker is activated.
  2. Switch the server to build v2 and call registration.update().
  3. Assert a worker is waiting and the update prompt appears; click it.
  4. Wait for controllerchange, then assert the page shows v2 and old caches are deleted.
  5. Set the context offline and assert the cached shell still loads.

Keep the fetch handlers' logic in plain functions so they can also be unit-tested.

code.title: Cache-first, network-first with timeout, stale-while-revalidate

followUps:
Race the network request against a timer; if the timer wins, answer from the cache.

Use 2 to 3 seconds as a starting point: long enough for a normal connection, short enough that a bad network does not look frozen. Let the original fetch keep running (inside event.waitUntil) so it still refreshes the cache for next time, or cancel it with AbortController.

const timer = new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(rej, 3000));
try { return await Promise.race([fetch(req), timer]); }
catch { return (await caches.match(req)) || offlinePage; }

The cache lives on the user's device and outlives the login, so private data can be seen by the next person or served to the wrong account.

  • On a shared computer, a cached account page can be read after logout.
  • If the cache key is only the URL, user A's /api/me response can be returned to user B on the same browser.
  • Tokens or personal data may be stored longer than intended.

Mitigations: never cache responses marked Cache-Control: private or no-store, or requests with credentials; include the user id in the key if you must; call caches.delete() on logout; keep payments network-only.

code.title: Offline outbox: retry with backoff, dead letters, idempotent resend

followUps:
Decide the rule in advance and make the server detect it: a delete should leave a tombstone (a marker with a version), so a later edit from a stale device is recognised as a conflict, not silently lost.

The server answers the late edit with a conflict (for example HTTP 409 plus the deleted state). For notes, the safest default is "edit wins": restore the item with the user's text so nothing typed is lost, and tell the user "this was deleted on another device, restored". For other data you may ask instead. Keep tombstones long enough (say 30 to 90 days) that a device offline for weeks still learns about the delete.

Use IndexedDB's own version number. When you open the database with a higher version, the browser runs onupgradeneeded, where you apply the migrations step by step.

req.onupgradeneeded = (e) => {
  const db = req.result;
  if (e.oldVersion < 2) db.createObjectStore("outbox", { keyPath: "id" });
  if (e.oldVersion < 3) req.transaction.objectStore("notes").createIndex("by_updated", "updatedAt");
};

Test an upgrade from every old version. Handle onversionchange so an old tab closes its connection instead of blocking the upgrade. Also convert queued outbox messages to the new shape.

code.title: Plural categories with Intl.PluralRules vs the naive ternary

followUps:
It only works for English-like languages. Other languages have more plural forms, and even English-like rules differ for zero.

Russian has four categories: 1 file is "файл" (one), 2 is "файла" (few), 5 is "файлов" (many), and 21 is again "one". Arabic has six categories (zero, one, two, few, many, other). The ternary also hard-codes English words, so translators cannot change them. Use ICU messages, such as {count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}, or Intl.PluralRules, and let each language's catalog define its own forms.

A mismatch happens when the server and the browser format the same date differently, because they use different time zones or locales. React then warns, or repaints with different text.

Fixes: format the first render deterministically on both sides (for example UTC with an explicit locale taken from the request), then switch to the user's time zone in an effect after mount. Or send an ISO string and format only on the client, marking that element with suppressHydrationWarning. Avoid calling new Date() during render: "5 minutes ago" will differ between server and client.

code.title: Stable percentage rollout with FNV-1a buckets

followUps:
Because Math.random() gives a new answer each time, so the same user would flip between old and new on every page load.

With a 10% rollout and random choice, someone who visits 20 times sees the new version about twice, in random places. The server and browser would disagree, you could not tell which users saw what when analysing an experiment, and you could not reproduce a bug report. A hash of flag key plus user id always gives the same bucket, with no storage needed, and it works the same on every server.

Use the same hash, but split the bucket range, and give each experiment its own salt so assignments are independent.

For one experiment with three variants, use 10,000 buckets: below 3,334 is A, below 6,667 is B, otherwise C. Include the experiment key in the hash (exp-42:user-7), so being in A of experiment 42 says nothing about experiment 43. If experiments must never overlap (they change the same page), put them in a layer: hash with the layer key, then give each experiment a separate range of buckets.

int b = hash("exp-42:" + userId) % 10000;
String v = b < 3334 ? "A" : b < 6667 ? "B" : "C";

Pick a few numbers before the change and check them again after, for both the delivery speed and the quality.

  • Per-team deploy frequency and lead time for change; change-failure rate and time to restore.
  • CI time (p50 and p90) and cache hit rate; pull request wait time; merge conflicts.
  • How often one team's release is blocked by another team.
  • Bundle size per route and the number of duplicated libraries on a page.

Write targets into the ADR, for example "CI p90 under 15 minutes; every team ships weekly on its own". If the numbers do not move by the revisit date, change the design.

Set budgets per remote and measure real users per remote, so a regression is traced to the team that shipped it.

  • Enforce size and lab-LCP budgets in each remote's CI.
  • Share framework singletons so React is not downloaded twice.
  • Preload the remote entry for the current route so it does not load as a waterfall after the shell.
  • Reserve fixed space (skeleton) for each remote to avoid layout shift.
  • Tag RUM data (LCP, INP, CLS) with the remote name; canary new versions and roll back automatically on a regression.

Anything where a silent mistake is costly or cannot be undone: I would always have a human review these in detail.

  • Authentication, sessions, permissions, payment and personal-data flows.
  • Security configuration (CSP, CORS) and adding new dependencies (supply-chain risk).
  • Service worker caching rules and sync or conflict code, where bugs show as stale or lost data.
  • Database or local-storage migrations.
  • Architecture boundaries, and the tests that are supposed to guard all of the above.

Generated code can look right and still be wrong in these places, so review it as untrusted.

Compare outcomes before and after, using a baseline, and avoid vanity numbers such as lines written or suggestions accepted.

Useful measures: change-failure rate, bugs escaping to production, revert rate, review time and pull request size, accessibility and lint violations per 1,000 lines, and design-system adoption (count of raw hex colours or one-off components). Label AI-assisted pull requests, track for a quarter, and compare with the previous quarter or a similar team. Add a short developer survey. Be careful: other changes at the same time can distort the result.
